title: 25 — Design a Real-time Gaming Leaderboard
html:
25 — Design a Real-time Gaming Leaderboard

The one idea: a relational ORDER BY score over millions of rows on every request doesn't scale. A Redis sorted set keeps members ordered by score in a skip list: update and rank are O(log n), top-k is O(log n + k). Persist to a database for durability; the sorted set is the serving structure.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Top 10 players; a user's own rank (and optionally ±4 neighbours).
  • Score updates when a user wins a match (+1 point); leaderboard resets monthly.
  • 5M DAU, 25M MAU; real-time updates.

Estimates: 5M DAU × 10 games/day ÷ 10^5 ≈ 500 score updates/s, peak ~2,500/s; top-10 fetches ~50 QPS (once per game open).

Step 2 — High-level design

API

POST /v1/scores                { user_id, points }        -- internal, called by game servers only
GET  /v1/scores                                           -- top 10
GET  /v1/scores/{user_id}                                 -- rank + score

⚠️ Scores are set by the game server, never directly by the client — otherwise anyone can post a million points.

---
title: Leaderboard — high-level architecture
---
flowchart LR
    Client["Game client"] --> GS["Game service"]
    GS -->|"win → +1"| LS["Leaderboard service"]
    LS --> R[("Redis sorted set<br/>leaderboard_2026_09")]
    LS --> DB[("DB<br/>user profiles, score history")]
    Client -->|"view leaderboard"| LS

For very large scale or decoupling, game service → Kafka → leaderboard service (and analytics, push notifications, etc.).

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Why not the relational DB?

SELECT user_id, score, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) FROM leaderboard …

Needs a full scan/sort (or index walk) to compute rank for arbitrary users → too slow with millions of changing rows. Fine at small scale — say so.

3.2 Redis sorted set

Internally: a hash table (member → score) + a skip list (ordered by score).

Operation Command Complexity
Add points ZINCRBY leaderboard_2026_09 1 user42 O(log n)
Top 10 ZREVRANGE leaderboard_2026_09 0 9 WITHSCORES O(log n + 10)
User rank ZREVRANK leaderboard_2026_09 user42 O(log n)
Neighbours ZREVRANGE … rank-4 rank+4 O(log n + 9)

Monthly reset: a new key per month (leaderboard_YYYY_MM); old ones archived to the DB and expired.

Memory: 25M users × (~24 B ID + 8 B score + skip-list overhead ~2×) ≈ ~1–2 GB → one Redis node; add a replica for failover and read scaling.

Persistence: Redis AOF/RDB + the source of truth in the DB (point_history table) so the sorted set can be rebuilt.

3.3 Hydrating the top 10

Store user profile (name, avatar) in a Redis hash or cache; fetch in one MGET/pipeline after getting the IDs.

3.4 Ties

Same score → order by who reached it first. Encode as a composite score: score × 10^10 + (MAX_TS − timestamp), or keep a secondary hash of timestamps.

3.5 Scaling to 500M DAU

  • Fixed partitions by score range (shard 1: 1–100 points, shard 2: 101–200…): top-k from the highest shard; a user's rank = rank within shard + counts of all higher shards. Moving users between shards when their score crosses a boundary adds complexity.
  • Hash partitions (Redis Cluster): writes spread evenly, but top-k needs scatter-gather across all shards and exact rank for a user is expensive → offer percentile ranks instead.

3.6 Alternative: NoSQL

DynamoDB-style with a GSI on (game_month, score) and write sharding on the partition key — workable but more complex than Redis for exact rank.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Sorted set as the serving structure, DB for durability, monthly keys, game-server-authoritative scoring, ties, and sharding options with their rank-accuracy trade-offs.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Azure Cache for Redis with StackExchange.Redis:
IDatabase db = redis.GetDatabase();
string key = $"leaderboard_{DateTime.UtcNow:yyyy_MM}";

await db.SortedSetIncrementAsync(key, userId, 1);
SortedSetEntry[] top = await db.SortedSetRangeByRankWithScoresAsync(key, 0, 9, Order.Descending);
long? rank = await db.SortedSetRankAsync(key, userId, Order.Descending);   // 0-based
  • Durability: Azure SQL PointHistory table written in the same request (or via Service Bus) — rebuild the set from it if Redis is lost.
  • Real-time push of leaderboard changes: SignalR group per leaderboard.
  • Anti-cheat: score updates only through an authenticated server-to-server API (managed identity / client credentials), never from the game client.

Review checklist

  • Why SQL ORDER BY doesn't scale for arbitrary rank queries.
  • Sorted set operations with complexities.
  • Server-authoritative scores.
  • Monthly keys; durability via DB.
  • Ties.
  • Sharding strategy and its effect on exact rank.
